title: David Warner Pleads Guilty to Drink-Driving, Faces Possible Jail Term
excerpt: The former Australian Test opener admitted to a mid-range drink-driving offence in a Sydney court and will be sentenced on August 18.
body:
• David Warner has formally pleaded guilty to mid-range drink-driving after recording a blood alcohol reading of 0.104 — more than double the legal limit — during a random breath test in Sydney on Easter Sunday.
  • Sentencing is scheduled for August 18, with the 39-year-old facing potential penalties including a fine, licence disqualification, and up to nine months in prison.
  • Warner did not appear in court personally; his lawyer Bobby Hill previously described the decision to drive as "reckless" and "foolish."
  • The guilty plea threatens Warner's captaincy of the Sydney Thunder, given Cricket NSW's long-standing partnership with Transport for NSW on road safety.

Former Australian cricket star David Warner has pleaded guilty to a mid-range drink-driving charge in a Sydney court, ending months of legal proceedings that began when he was pulled over during a random breath test on Easter Sunday.

Warner, 39, was stopped by police on April 5 after his van was seen parking short of a roadside testing site at Maroubra in Sydney's east. He returned a positive result and was taken to Maroubra Police Station, where a second test recorded a blood alcohol concentration of 0.104 — more than double the legal limit of 0.05 in New South Wales.

A 'Reckless' Decision

Warner did not appear in person during the court proceedings. His defence lawyer Bobby Hill had previously told reporters that the former opener acknowledged his mistake after consuming three glasses of wine at a friend's apartment before deciding to drive rather than take an Uber.

"He knows what he did was wrong. He accepts that was a reckless decision, a foolish decision to get in his car instead of taking an Uber."

— Bobby Hill, Warner's defence lawyer

Hill had also pointed to the broader lesson of the case, noting the difficulty of self-assessing blood alcohol levels. "It doesn't matter if you're a tradesman, a doctor or one of the best opening batsmen in the world, that danger exists for every one of us," he said.

What Warner Faces at Sentencing

Sentencing has been scheduled for August 18. Under NSW law, a mid-range prescribed concentration of alcohol offence — which applies to drivers recording a BAC between 0.08 and 0.149 — carries penalties including a fine of up to A$2,200, automatic licence disqualification, mandatory participation in alcohol education programs, and a maximum prison sentence of nine months.

While first-time offenders typically receive fines and licence suspensions rather than custodial sentences, the severity of Warner's reading and the high-profile nature of the case will draw scrutiny at his sentencing hearing.

Captaincy in Doubt

The guilty plea has reignited questions about Warner's future as captain of the Sydney Thunder in Australia's Big Bash League. Cricket NSW has maintained a 23-year partnership with Transport for NSW, with the annual match between the Thunder and Brisbane Heat named the Road Safety Cup — one of the state's most prominent road safety platforms.

Cricket NSW CEO Lee Germon had earlier said the captaincy decision "remains to be seen," while emphasising that the organisation takes such incidents "very seriously." Warner signed a one-year contract extension with the Thunder in January to play on past the age of 40 in the upcoming BBL season.

"The allegations, of course, are concerning and we take them very seriously. At Cricket NSW, we are strong advocates for safe driving, not drink-driving."

— Lee Germon, Cricket NSW CEO

A Career of Highs and Controversies

Warner retired from international cricket in 2024 after amassing 8,786 runs in 112 Tests at an average above 44, including a career-best 335 not out against Pakistan. He also appeared in 161 ODIs and 110 T20 Internationals, and was part of Australia's World Cup-winning squads in 2015 and 2023.

The drink-driving case is the latest in a series of off-field controversies for Warner, who was banned for a year and stripped of the vice-captaincy following the 2018 ball-tampering scandal in South Africa. He was also fined and suspended after punching England's Joe Root in a Birmingham bar during the 2013 Champions Trophy.

Despite his legal troubles, Warner has continued to perform at the highest level in franchise cricket. He averaged 86.6 for the Sydney Thunder in the most recent BBL season and was named captain of the tournament's official team of the season. He also captained Karachi Kings in the Pakistan Super League earlier this year, averaging 51.2 across seven matches.

What Happens Next

Warner's sentencing on August 18 will determine the exact penalties he faces. The outcome could also influence whether Cricket NSW retains him as Thunder captain — a decision that carries significant commercial and reputational weight given the franchise's road safety commitments. For Indian cricket fans, Warner remains a familiar figure from his stints as captain of SunRisers Hyderabad in the IPL, where he led the franchise to its maiden title in 2016.
